extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, and literary critics evaluating or writing dramatic poetry (English stage)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging or composing dramatic poetry for the English stage — focusing on language, wit, conversation, and adaptation to the contemporary age. The essay argues how plays should conform to and improve upon the manners and speech of their time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity of genius to the age
rubrics_metrics.description: They, who have best succeeded on the stage, Have still conformed their genius to their age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful dramatist matches their work to the tastes, manners, and conversational habits of their own age. Examples: Jonson suited 'mechanic humour' to a duller age; past successes depended on pleasing contemporary audiences. Anti-pattern: writing that harkens only to antiquated fashions without regard for present sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement of wit
rubrics_metrics.description: An improvement of our Wit ... (part of 'refinement'). 'Wit's now arrived to a more high degree.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic poetry should display a higher degree of wit than earlier ages. Wit here implies lively, intelligent verbal play and inventive thought suited to contemporary conversation and taste. Works should aim for sharper, more refined wit than predecessors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refinement of language
rubrics_metrics.description: Our native language more refined and free; 'An improvement of our ... Language.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of language should be more correct, pleasing, and significant than in previous ages. This includes avoiding solecisms and gross flaws in sense. The author claims present writers have fewer and less gross improprieties and that language should be improved rather than slavishly imitating older usages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refinement of conversation (natural dialogue)
rubrics_metrics.description: An improvement of our ... Conversation; 'Our ladies and our men now speak more wit In conversation, than those poets writ.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialogue should reflect the refined, lively conversation of the age; characters' speech should feel natural and current. Playwrights should model dialogue on contemporary conversational usage rather than arch or antiquated speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject improper/ill-sounding words and phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: The refinement consists in 'either in rejecting such old words, or phrases, which are ill sounding, or improper.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately omit archaic or awkward words/phrases that sound bad or are improper in sense. Preference should be given to clarity and euphony. Anti-pattern: preserving antiquated diction merely from reverence for the past.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admit new words/phrases that are more proper and significant
rubrics_metrics.description: The refinement consists ... or in admitting new, which are more proper, more sounding, and more significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to incorporating new, apt expressions that improve clarity, sound, or meaning. Innovation in diction that better conveys sense and feeling is a mark of progress in dramatic language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical awareness: observe errors to correct them
rubrics_metrics.description: One testimony ... that we are the first who have observed them; and, certainly, to observe errors is a great step to the correcting of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and critics must be able to detect solecisms and flaws in earlier writing; recognition of faults is prerequisite to improving dramatic practice. Encourages self-critique and editorial correction rather than complacency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not accept antiquity on trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Antiquity alone is no plea for the excellency of a poem; the last (if equal in wit) has the advantage of knowing more and better than the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate older works on their merits, but do not treat age or tradition as automatic justification. Preference may be given to improvements that advance the art relative to past models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid coarseness even if formerly acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: Then comedy was faultless, but 'twas coarse ... And, as their comedy, their love was mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What passed as acceptable humor or subject-matter in a less refined age (coarse jokes, mean situations) should be avoided if public taste has become more refined. Strive for elevated manners and avoid low or vulgar comedic effects when they no longer suit the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision of craft: attend to each line and every word
rubrics_metrics.description: When critics weigh Each line, and every word, throughout a play, None of them, no not Jonson in his height, Could pass, without allowing grains for weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights should craft lines carefully — expect close critical scrutiny of diction and phrasing. Ambition: produce work that withstands line-by-line critical examination; be economical and exact in expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance reverence for past merits with demand for progress
rubrics_metrics.description: I would ascribe to dead authors their just praises ... and in those wherein we contend with them for the pre-eminence, I would acknowledge our advantages to the age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fair critical stance credits past authors where deserved but also claims legitimate improvements for the present. Do not reject predecessors wholesale; praise where due, but also argue for the advances of current practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for progress so poetry does not go backward
rubrics_metrics.description: My ambition in this essay, than that poetry may not go backward, when all other arts and sciences are advancing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The playwright's responsibility is to contribute to the advancement of dramatic art, aligning its development with broader cultural and intellectual progress. Anti-pattern: complacency that preserves old forms at the cost of artistic development.
